title: The beginning (Mark 1:1–8)
hookLine: no birth story: Mark starts with a voice in the wilderness and a man in camel hair
carry: the beginning of the good news

lines: NO MANGER, NO ANGELS, NO BABY.
cards: If you know the Christmas story, you might expect a book about Jesus to start there: the manger, the shepherds, the star. Mark doesn't. No manger, no angels singing, no wise men, no baby at all.
It opens with one line, like a title, and drops you straight into the desert, where a wild-looking man in camel hair is shouting at crowds by a river.
For the next several weeks: Mark from the beginning, a few verses at a time.

teach.b: Mark begins, in the King James Bible: "The beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God."
Gospel is an Old English word, godspel, good news, translating the Greek euangelion. And here's what first readers would have heard.
In the Roman world, euangelion was the word for big public announcements: a victory in battle, a new emperor.
An inscription from a city in what's now Turkey even calls the emperor Augustus's birthday the beginning of good news for the world. So Mark's opening is a bold claim: the real good news is this.
Then he quotes the prophets: "The voice of one crying in the wilderness, Prepare ye the way of the Lord, make his paths straight." And there's the voice: John the Baptist.
Mark gives his outfit and his menu: "John was clothed with camel's hair, and with a girdle of a skin about his loins; and he did eat locusts and wild honey." That's not a random detail.
The book of Kings remembers the prophet Elijah as a hairy man with a leather belt, and Malachi said Elijah would be sent before the great day of the Lord. Mark's readers would have noticed.
Crowds come from all over Judea and Jerusalem to be baptized by John in the Jordan.
But John points away from himself: "There cometh one mightier than I after me, the latchet of whose shoes I am not worthy to stoop down and unloose." Eight verses, and Mark is already racing.
That's his style: no lingering, just the sense that something is starting, right now.

how: In many churches, a passage from the Gospels is read aloud at every service, often with the congregation standing, and many Christians read through a gospel like Mark in order, a few verses a day.

games.q: what's inside the opening — tap the pairs.
p: camel hair and a leather belt

s: Mark's gospel begins with the birth of Jesus
Mark has no birth story. it opens in the wilderness with John the Baptist.
Mark calls his book good news in its first line
its first words are: the beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ.
John's camel hair and belt are random details
they echo Elijah, whom Malachi said God would send before the great day.

games.q: you're John the Baptist. crowds from all Judea and Jerusalem are coming to you. what do you tell them about yourself?
o: that you are the one they've been waiting for.
that one mightier is coming, and you're not worthy to untie his shoes.
that they should follow you into the desert.
games.why: "there cometh one mightier than I after me." John's whole job is to point away from himself.

practice: Open to Mark chapter one if you have a Bible or an app nearby, and read the first eight verses slowly, out loud; if not, just hold the first line in your mind.
Notice how fast it moves: a title, a prophecy, a voice, a man in camel hair, crowds, a river, and someone mightier coming.
Then sit with whichever image stayed with you, offering it back if you pray, or just letting it sit if you don't.

wordCard.voice: Gospel. From Old English for good news, translating the Greek euangelion, a word once used for an emperor's announcements.

orig.note: Greek: the beginning of the good news — the first words of Mark.
